newsitem.title: UK: Sovereign ceiling can be breached, Fitch Says.
newsitem.headline: Sovereign ceiling can be breached, Fitch Says.

text.p: Certain foreign currency-denominated debt issues can be rated higher than their sovereigns, based on newly published criteria, says Fitch Investors Service.
The action is most relevant to emerging market debt issuers in Asia, Latin America and former Soviet Eastern block countries.
Companies there last year issued $187.4 billion of debt and volume is growing. In this year's first quarter, 329 issues totaling $53.6 billion were marketed.

Details appear in a new report, ''Rating Unsecured Debt Denominated in Foreign Currency,'' by Neil Baron, vice chairman and general counsel, Peter Jordan, managing director and Gabriel Torres, director, of Fitch's International Ratings Group.

Exporters and business partners, and affiliates of strong multinational corporations are the most likely candidates for higher ratings because they can mitigate the risks of currency devaluation, foreign exchange controls, expropriation, nationalization and repudiation. Using this analysis, for example, a Mexican bottler for The Coca-Cola Co. and subsidiaries of Kimberly-Clark Corp. and Nestle SA have received debt ratings that are higher than Mexico's.

Exporters can benefit from external receivables by submitting to the jurisdiction of courts in highly-rated countries, agreeing to be bound by their laws and limiting debt to a small percentage of outstanding receivables.

A country's historical respect for legal, contractual and property rights will also affect these ratings. Fitch's views on rating foreign currency unsecured debt are part of a major project examining how country conditions affect ratings of nonsovereign issues outside the U.S. For information, call Neil Baron 212-908-0509, Gabriel Torres 212-908-0705 or Peter Jordan 212-908-0566.
